title: Fragmented surge: latency vs $/query portrait (draft)
content:
Goal: produce a concise, reproducible snapshot comparing latency percentiles and dollars-per-query across a small set of realistic workload morphologies focused on session fragmentation (many short sessions interleaved with sparse long sessions). This is a working draft intended for product + platform discussion; numbers are from lab runs on a single-region dev cluster (r5-equivalent GPU pool), not production telemetry.

Key questions:
- How does session fragmentation (fraction of short sessions) change p50/p90/p99 latency and unit cost under three serving configs: baseline (FP16, no caching), kv-cache-prefetch (KV cache warm-up), and compact-quant (8-bit quantized kernels)?
- Are there sweet spots where small increases in p50 yield >10% cost savings at p90/p99 tolerances?
- Which metrics should product display to customers to make the tradeoff visible?

Methodology (short):
- Synthetic driver generates sessions with fixed message length distribution: short (mean tokens 12, 85% of sessions), medium (mean 64, 13%), long (mean 240, 2%).
- Session fragmentation parameter f = fraction of short sessions that arrive with 30–120s idle between messages (creates cold-kv scenarios). We sweep f = [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9].
- Serving configs: baseline (FP16, no kv prefetch), kv-prefetch (FP16 + on-request KV warm-up heuristic), compact-quant (8-bit kernel, slightly higher per-token throughput but lower memory headroom).
- Each run: 10k sessions, steady-state injection rate equivalent to average of 150 QPS. We capture p50/p90/p99 for response latency and compute cost-per-query using local cost model (GPU-minute + memory overhead amortized).

Representative numeric table (aggregated):

Scenario | f (short-frag) | Config | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | $/query (micro)
-------- | -------------- | ------ | ------- | ------- | ------- | -----------
Base     | 0.0            | baseline      | 72      | 210     | 470     | 18.4
Base     | 0.5            | baseline      | 85      | 320     | 920     | 20.2
Base     | 0.9            | baseline      | 95      | 430     | 1400    | 22.1
KVpref   | 0.5            | kv-prefetch   | 80      | 250     | 580     | 19.3
KVpref   | 0.9            | kv-prefetch   | 88      | 300     | 760     | 20.0
Quant    | 0.5            | compact-quant | 110     | 360     | 760     | 15.6
Quant    | 0.9            | compact-quant | 120     | 420     | 980     | 16.2

Interpretation notes:
- Fragmentation increases both latency percentiles and unit cost in baseline because cold-KV fills and lower packing efficiency drive more GPU time per query.
- KV-prefetch reduces p90/p99 tail significantly for mid-fragmentation scenarios (f around 0.5) but has diminishing returns at extreme fragmentation where prefetch heuristics misfire on very sparse sessions.
- Compact quant reduces $/query materially (~15–25%) at the expense of higher p50 (in this dataset p50 increases ~25–40ms) due to quant kernel overheads and slightly higher token decode latency. However, p99 impact is smaller than baseline: quant's reduced per-token cost allows higher concurrency without changing GPU footprint.

Ascii sparkline summary (p90 vs $/query tradeoff):
- baseline    p90: [210, 320, 430]  $/q: [18.4, 20.2, 22.1]
- kv-prefetch p90: [200, 250, 300]  $/q: [18.9, 19.3, 20.0]
- quant       p90: [260, 360, 420]  $/q: [16.0, 15.6, 16.2]

Mini-plot (normalized axes; lower is better for both):
- baseline:  ╭───╮         ╭────╮         ╭──────╮
            p90=210      p90=320      p90=430
            $  =18.4     $  =20.2     $  =22.1
- kv-prefetch: ╭──╮    ╭───╮    ╭────╮
               p90=200 p90=250 p90=300
               $  =18.9  $=19.3  $=20.0
- quant:       ╭────╮      ╭─────╮      ╭─────╮
               p90=260     p90=360     p90=420
               $  =16.0     $=15.6      $=16.2

Tradeoff framing for product:
- If a customer cares mostly about p90/p99 SLOs for conversational UX (low tail jitter), kv-prefetch is a low-risk knob: small cost bump, large tail improvement at moderate fragmentation.
- If cost-per-query is primary and p50 is the main touchpoint (e.g., batch completion or non-interactive use), compact quant is compelling: 15–25% savings versus baseline but expect higher median latency (per-user perception could degrade for low-latency interactions).
- For extreme fragmentation (f >= 0.9) no single knob is a panacea: mixing strategies (light prefetch + quant) and admission control (prioritize warm sessions) are likely necessary.

Recommendations / next steps (product + infra experiment plan):
1) Run A/B in a small customer cohort with: baseline vs kv-prefetch (enable only for sessions with >2 messages historically). Metric: p90 for conversational routes, cost delta, user dropoff.
2) Controlled lab stress test: combine quant + kv-prefetch to measure compound effects (we expect quant to absorb throughput but leave tail dependent on cache warmup behavior).
3) Telemetry surfaces: add an \"fragmentation score\" to the Console (per-application) that reports: fraction short sessions, observed kv-miss rate, p90 delta vs baseline, estimated $/query impact.
4) UX copy for Console: present three labeled modes and rough guidance: \"Low-latency (baseline with warm affinity)\", \"Tail-optimized (kv-prefetch)\", \"Cost-optimized (compact-quant)\" with icons and expected percentile bands.

Open questions / caveats:
- Our cost model is simplified (single-region GPU amortization). Multi-region and reserved capacity dynamics will change break-even points.
- Real user traffic has richer correlations (session stickiness, retry patterns) that can make prefetch heuristics more or less effective.
- Quantization effects depend on specific model architecture; some models show larger inference latency regressions under 8-bit kernels. We should test across 2–3 representative models.

Appendix: quick-run steps to reproduce locally
1) checkout: git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/optimize && cd optimize/bench
2) driver: python run_fragmentation_sweep.py --seed 42 --sessions 10000 --qps 150 --frags 0.0,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.9 --configs baseline,kvprefetch,compactquant
3) analyzer: python summarize_results.py --input runs/frag_sweep/*.json --output summary-frag-2028-03-14.txt

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally compact; if we go forward I'll convert the numeric tables into Console-ready visualizations (heatmap and a two-axis scatter with p90 on x and $/query on y) and expand runs to include reserved capacity curves.
